title: Persisted or exchanged binary data without an evolution contract
pattern: Cross-version messages or durable records depend on raw memory layout, positional field order, or language-specific object serialization (e.g., Java Serialization, Python pickle, raw C struct casting) without a compatible schema/version contract.
why_bad: Changes to field order, alignment, names, or shape can break old data and rolling upgrades: adding an optional field, reordering elements, or renaming a member corrupts historical serializations, causes immediate deserialization errors, and prevents independent reader/writer upgrades.
detection: Flag any of: (1) byte packing logic that writes record attributes sequentially without pre-assigned tag numbers, field names, or a global format version; (2) raw byte pointers cast directly to struct types (`unsafe { &*(bytes.as_ptr() as *const NetworkPayload) }`) for network or persisted data; (3) a serialization library or codec lacking field tags or the structural tolerance needed for independent reader/writer upgrades.
counterexample:
```rust
// Valid: tag-based serialization or explicit versioning
#[derive(serde::Serialize, serde::Deserialize)]
struct TrackDTOV2 {
    #[serde(rename = "v")]
    version: u32,
    title: String,
    performers: Vec<String>,
}
```
Also valid: ephemeral same-binary, same-layout intra-process data or memory-mapped files where reader and writer are compiled into the exact same binary, provided representation and memory-safety requirements are satisfied; or a codec with an explicit supported compatibility contract.
fix: Use a versioned envelope (carrying an integer schema version) with dispatch/migration logic, or a schema-driven tagged codec with defined evolution rules (Protobuf, Avro, Thrift) that permits ignored or added fields. Self-describing formats like JSON/MessagePack can help, but still require explicit handling of added/removed fields and type changes; merely adding a version field does not by itself implement compatibility.
source: *Martin Fowler - Patterns of Enterprise Application Architecture (2002)*, page 401; *Vaughn Vernon - Implementing Domain-Driven Design (2013)*, Chapter 14; Patterns of Enterprise Application Architecture, "Assembling a Data Transfer Object" [828]; Designing Data-Intensive Applications, Chapter 4, "Programming-language-specific encodings" [187, 653]
